title: Security & Compliance — RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows
author: Sofia Nguyen
body:
Overview:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s security and compliance controls and operational workflows for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging and log retention, data residency and retention requirements, secure SDLC gates, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence generation/collection, and risk & exceptions handling. It is intended for engineering, security, product, and compliance stakeholders implementing or auditing production and private deployments.

Goals:
- Establish consistent RBAC and auth patterns across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Ensure auditability of user and system actions with centralized logging and tamper-resistance.
- Define clear data residency and retention defaults and exceptions process.
- Bake security gates into the SDLC with measurable evidence artifacts.
- Standardize incident response steps for security-sensitive incidents.
- Provide a reproducible compliance evidence workflow for SOC2/ISO audits.
- Document risk acceptance and exception processes with owners and timelines.

1) RBAC and Authentication
Summary:
Redwood uses role-based access control for the console, control plane APIs, and customer private deployments. Authentication is delegated to enterprise identity providers (IdP) where possible (OIDC/SAML). For machine-to-machine, we use short-lived service tokens and mTLS for internal services.

Primary roles and responsibilities (minimum):
- security-admin: full security configuration, audit, and exception approval.
- infra-admin: infrastructure lifecycle operations, terraform/apply (no data access by default).
- platform-engineer: deploy and operate serving runtime, limited customer config changes.
- support-agent: access to support tooling with scoped access and session recording.
- read-only-auditor: view-only access to logs, dashboards, and policy docs.

RBAC rules / examples:
- Console and API: least privilege by default. Every new role request must include justification and expiry.
- Privileged actions (key material export, DB backups, KMS rekey) require two-person approval and are logged as privileged sessions.
- Service accounts: scoped to actions (e.g., batch-ingest, model-import) and issued with TTL <= 24h when issuing short-lived tokens.

Authentication specifics:
- IdP: SSO via SAML/OIDC (Okta primary). Default MFA required for interactive users (TOTP/U2F).
- Service auth: mTLS between services; short-lived JWT for cross-service API calls.
- Key material: customer keys (Private deployments) integrate with customer KMS/HSM (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or on-prem HSM).

Provisioning process (high-level):
1. Request via Access Request UI (GitHub or Console form).
2. Manager + Owner approval.
3. Security review for privileged roles.
4. Automated provisioning via IAM automation (audit entry written).

2) Audit Logging
Logging objectives:
- Capture authentication, authorization decisions, admin actions, configuration changes, and data access events.
- Ensure logs are centralized, integrity-protected, and retained per compliance requirements.

Log pipeline and storage:
- Sources: Console, Control Plane APIs, Serving Runtime (request/response metadata and model variant routing), K8s control plane events (for managed clusters), and customer connectors (private deployments).
- Collector: Fluentd -> Kafka (internal) -> SIEM ingestion.
- SIEM: Splunk (hosted) for indexing, alerting, and long-term retention for critical logs.
- Immutable archive: Encrypted object storage with write-once lifecycle for audit-grade logs (retention enforced via policy).

Retention & protection:
- Authentication & authorization events: 7 years (SOC2/enterprise requirement) — stored in SIEM + immutable archive.
- Admin/config changes & deployment events: 3 years.
- Application-level request traces (non-PII request metadata): 365 days.
- Sensitive data and PII logs: redacted at source, retained per customer-specific agreements.

Integrity controls:
- Logs are signed using HMAC before archive; signing keys rotated quarterly and stored in KMS.
- Access to raw log archives is restricted to security-admin and compliance-admin roles with JIT approval.

Example audit queries and alerts:
- Failed privileged action attempts > 3 in 10 minutes -> high-priority alert to SEC oncall.
- Unexpected KMS key policy change -> immediate high-severity pager.
- New external ingress to private deployment -> audit trail and incident runbook trigger.

3) Data Residency and Retention
Default residency model:
- Hosted (Redwood-managed): customer data stored in region selected at account creation (US, EU, APAC).
- Dedicated: data stored in customer-dedicated project/region per contract.
- Private: customer-managed and complies with their own residency controls.

Default retention periods (unless contractual override):
| Data class | Typical storage location | Retention |
|---|---|---|
| Auth events | SIEM | 7 years |
| Admin / infra audit logs | SIEM + archive | 3 years |
| Request metadata (non-PII) | Observability store | 1 year |
| Model artifacts (customer-owned) | Object store | per customer SLA |
| PII / Sensitive input data | Encrypted customer bucket | per customer agreement / purged on request |

Data deletion / erasure process:
1. Customer submits GDPR/CCPA request via Console or Support ticket.
2. Data mapping executed by Data Privacy team; affected storage locations enumerated.
3. Erasure tasks queued and executed with audit trail and confirmation to customer.
4. For backups/archives, erasure may be logical until retention windows expire; this is documented to customers at time of onboarding.

4) Secure SDLC (DevSecOps Gates)
Security gates integrated into CI/CD and release processes:
- Static Analysis (SAST): required on all pull requests. Issues classified P0-P3. P0/P1 block merge until remediated or risk accepted.
- Dependency Scanning: automated dependency scanning with SBOM generation; critical vulnerabilities must be remediated within SLA (14 days for critical).
- Secrets Detection: pre-commit hook + CI step; secrets found in PR cause failure and automatic rotation of implicated keys.
- Dynamic Scanning / Fuzzing: scheduled for public-facing surfaces and pre-release for major runtime changes.
- Threat Model & Design Review: required for high-impact changes (new data flows, private deployment features, key management changes).

Evidence artifacts produced per release:
- Build SBOM (software bill of materials) — stored in artifact registry.
- SAST report and remediation tickets.
- Dependency scan summary.
- Threat model document and sign-off (owner + security reviewer).

Release checklist (example):
1. Merge to main after passing CI and security gates.
2. Run release smoke tests in staging (automated).
3. Security reviewer sign-off for production rollout.
4. Create release tag and attach SBOM + SAST artifacts.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures
Scope & triggers:
- This section covers confidentiality, integrity, and availability incidents with security implications (exfiltration, unauthorized config changes, key compromise, severe data leakage).

Incident roles (brief):
- Incident Commander (IC): coordinates response and comms.
- Technical Lead: owns technical triage and mitigation.
- Security Investigator: performs forensic analysis and root cause.
- Legal & Privacy: customer notifications and regulatory decisions.
- Communications: external and internal comms templates.

Runbook (high-level):
1. Detect & Triage: SIEM alert/fan-in -> initial severity (P0-P3).
2. Contain: isolate affected systems (network ACLs, revoke keys, disable user sessions).
3. Preserve Evidence: snapshot VMs, export logs from SIEM, preserve access logs, collect forensic images.
4. Eradicate & Remediate: apply fixes, rotate keys, patch vulnerable components.
5. Recover: bring systems to validated state with canary traffic and monitoring.
6. Postmortem & Notification: 72-hour initial report for P0/P1 incidents; full postmortem within 30 days.

Forensic guidance:
- Use immutable export of logs and cryptographic checksums for chain-of-custody.
- Use separate forensic environment with read-only copies of artifacts.

Customer-facing incidents (private/dedicated):
- Notify affected customers within contract SLA (typically 72 hours for incidents with potential data impact).
- Provide evidence artifacts as agreed (redacted where necessary).

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows
Audit preparation:
- Map controls to evidence locations (control repo). Example: SOC2 CC6.1 (log retention) -> SIEM retention policy + archive manifest.
- Evidence owners are assigned per control (security, infra, platform, product).

Evidence collection steps (typical):
1. Initiate evidence request in Compliance Tracker (Jira project COMPLIANCE).
2. Evidence owner attaches artifacts (config exports, screenshots, log manifests, runbooks, access lists, screenshots of IAM roles).
3. Compliance team reviews and marks evidence as sufficient or requests additional items.
4. For on-site audits, prepare read-only consoles and pre-compiled evidence bundles.

Standard artifacts (non-exhaustive):
- IAM role definitions and change history (CSV export).
- Audit log retention policy and archive manifests (signed with archive checksum).
- SBOM and SAST reports for sample releases.
- Incident postmortem artifacts with redactions for sensitive customer data.
- Penetration test reports and remediation logs.

Retention of evidence bundles:
- Audit artifacts: retained for duration of certification cycle plus 2 years (typ. 3–5 years).

7) Risk & Exceptions
Risk acceptance process:
- Any permanent deviation from documented security controls requires a documented risk assessment and approval by Security and the owning team. Exceptions are timeboxed (default 90 days) and must include compensating controls.

Exception request flow:
1. Submit Exception Request in Exception Tracker (Jira EXCEPTIONS) with justification, mitigation, and owner.
2. Security reviews and assigns risk rating (Low/Medium/High).
3. Security + Product/Infra either approve with expiry or deny.
4. Approved exceptions are recorded with monitoring requirements and periodic re-evaluation (every 30 days).

Example compensating controls:
- If unable to rotate a key immediately, require IP restriction + session logging + owner JIT approval for privileged operations.

Ownership and escalation:
- Security owns exception registry and quarterly review.
- High risk exceptions escalate to CRO for executive approval.

Appendices and references:
- Commands & examples:
  - Export IAM roles: aws iam get-account-authorization-details --query 'RoleDetailList' > roles.json
  - Rotate signing keys (KMS): aws kms rotate-key --key-id <key-id>
  - SIEM query example: index=auth_events event_type=failed_login | stats count by user | where count > 3
